title: Oxidation-induced restructuring of copper sulfides for enhanced performance in CO2 electroreduction
abstract: The CO2 electroreduction reaction (CO2ER) is a reliable pathway that enables a balanced carbon cycle for sustainable development strategies. There are several major challenges, such as selectivity, efficiency, and stability of the electrocatalysts that need to be addressed for the widespread application of this in the reduction of CO2. Herein, we develop an oxide-modification of Cu1.81S particles supported on multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites (Cu1.81S@WMCNT-600-OD) through a facile in-situ crystallization strategy. This modification improves the electroreduction activity in the reduction CO2 to formate with a low onset-potential of -0.47 V vs RHE (overpotential= 0.25 V). In addition, the material used in preparing this catalyst is widely accessible at low cost. Among the electrocatalysts tested, Cu1.81S@WMCNT-600-OD exhibits a high CO2 selectivity towards formate at an overpotential of 0.45 V with high faradaic efficiency (82 %) for nearly 20 h. Further investigations reveal that the needle-like dendritic structure formed during electrolysis is the likely source for the improved performance in CO2 reduction. Therefore, this work provides low-cost, abundant, and efficient catalysts for CO2ER and a facile pathway that improves the electrocatalytic performance.

A B S T R A C T
The CO2 electroreduction reaction (CO2ER) is a reliable pathway that enables a balanced carbon cycle for sustainable development strategies. There are several major challenges, such as selectivity, efficiency, and stability of the electrocatalysts that need to be addressed for the widespread application of this in the reduction of CO2. Herein, we develop an oxide-modification of Cu1.81S particles supported on multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites (Cu1.81S@WMCNT-600-OD) through a facile in-situ crystallization strategy. This modification improves the electroreduction activity in the reduction CO2 to formate with a low onset-potential of -0.47 V vs RHE (overpotential= 0.25 V). In addition, the material used in preparing this catalyst is widely accessible at low cost. Among the electrocatalysts tested, Cu1.81S@WMCNT-600-OD exhibits a high CO2 selectivity towards formate at an overpotential of 0.45 V with high faradaic efficiency (82 %) for nearly 20 h. Further investigations reveal that the needle-like dendritic structure formed during electrolysis is the likely source for the improved performance in CO2 reduction. Therefore, this work provides low-cost, abundant, and efficient catalysts for CO2ER and a facile pathway that improves the electrocatalytic performance.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 powered by renewable sources (e.g. solar, wind) is a conceivable pathway to sustainably store energy in the form of valuable chemicals, such as carbon monoxide, formate/formic acid, hydrocarbons, aldehydes and alcohols [1–3]. However, significant energy barriers, and sluggish electron and proton transfer kinetics need to be overcome for the CO2 electroreduction reaction (CO2ER) to be viable, due to the high chemical stability of CO2. Furthermore, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which requires relatively low activation energy, is competitive with the CO2ER and leads to poor selectivity, especially in aqueous solutions. Therefore, it is essential to develop efficient and resourceful catalysts with high selectivity and long stability [4,5].
Generating formate/formic acid is one of the most feasible pathway for the CO2ER due to its low electron transfer requirements [6]. Conversion of CO2 to formic acid is widely used in multiple practical applications [7–9]. Traditional uses for formic acid include leather tanning, animal feed, and pharmaceutical production [10].When involved
in energy storage, formic acid is one of the most promising materials used to store liquid hydrogen due to its chemical stability, but it can be easily decomposed to H2 and CO2 with the assistance of catalysts [11].
The product distribution of the CO2ER is highly dependent on the nature of the electrode materials. Transition metals are attractive due to their remarkably high selectivity and efficient activity for the formation of formate [12]. Nevertheless, relatively high cost, scarcity, and environmental harmfulness discourage their large-scale application. Environmentally friendly metals with different nanoscale structures (nanorods, nanosheets, nanoparticles, etc.) have also been investigated as electrocatalysts for the CO2ER. Studies have shown that the conversion of CO2 to formic acid/formate was favored on non-noble metal surfaces, including In [13], Sn [14], Cd [15], Bi [16], Ti [17], Cu [18–20], and some of their oxides (e.g., SnO2 [21,22]). More recently, transition metal chalcogenides (TMCs) have been identified as promising candidates due to their low cost and rich abundance, and they have been widely studied in energy storage and water splitting applications, showing excellent performance [23–26]. Among the TMCs catalysts, copper sulfides, which exhibit various stoichiometric composition

ranges from Cu2S (copper rich) to CuS2 (sulfur rich) [27], were applied in supercapacitors [28] and the HER [29], in forms including CuS nanowires [30] and Cu7.2S4 sub-microspheres [31]. Recently, limited researches towards CO2ER were performed using CuxS [32]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there exist no investigations into the electrocatalytic performance of Cu1.81S in the CO2ER.
Bulk materials exhibit low current density and poor stability in aqueous electrolytes. Furthermore, slow mass transport and electron transfer ascribed to low specific surface area limit the CO2ER performance. Therefore, the combination of catalysts with conductive supports [16,33–36] has been proposed to increase the surface area and expose more active sites. Appropriate supports can also suppress the aggregation of catalyst particles, stabilize the loaded catalysts, and facilitate electron transfer. For example, multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) are a promising support due to their porous structure which can promote the transfer of reactants and enable the interactions between electrons and active sites of catalysts [21].
In this study, nanosized Cu1.81S microparticles, supported on the surface of commercial MWCNTs, were prepared through a facile twostep coupling approach. The hybrid catalyst was employed as a cathode for the CO2ER, showing an excellent onset-potential. In addition, the effect of copper oxides located on the surface of the Cu1.81S particles was investigated, since it has been reported that metal oxides deposited on the surface of metal catalysts suppress the HER, thereby enhancing the CO2ER [37]. It was found that partially oxidized Cu1.81S (denoted as Cu1.81S@WMCNTs-600-OD) was effective for the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. Cu1.81S@WMCNTs-600-OD remarkably enhanced the CO2ER with high Faradaic Efficiency toward formate, while also showing excellent stability over 20 h. Further evaluation of the microscopic surface restructuring revealed that needle-like dendritic shapes were formed during electrolysis.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Copper(II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, ≥99 %, Aladdin), rubeanic acid (N,N’-Bis(2-hydroxyethyl) dithiooxamide, ≥98.0 %, Tokyo Chemical Industry Co.,Ltd.), ethanol (CH3CH2OH, ≥99.8 %, Aladdin), deionized water (18.2 MΩ, Milli-Q water purification system), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, ≥99.99 %, Sigma-Aldrich), nafion solution (5 wt%, Shanghai He Sen Electric Co., Ltd.), formic acid (HCOOH, ≥99.5 %, Aladdin), dimethyl sulfoxide (C2H6OS, ≥99.95 %,Aladdin), and deuteroxide (D2O, 99.9atom%,Meryer Chemical Technology Co., Ltd.) were purchased and used without any further purification. Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT, ≥99 %, XFNANO Materials Tech Co., Ltd (Nanjing, China)) were added into an aqueous 1M H2SO4 solution, then heated to 60 °C to eliminate the impact of metal impurities, which are a well-known catalyst for CO2ER. Then the MWCNTs were rinsed with ultrapure H2O several times. After centrifugation and drying in air for 12 h, pretreated MWCNTs were stored for later use.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Pristine copper rubeane (CuRA)
sections.text:
CuRA was synthesized at room temperature. Briefly, an ethanol
solution with 50mM rubeanic acid and an aqueous solution with 50mM Cu(NO3)2·3H2O were mixed dropwise adding the former into the latter under vigorous stirring. Black precipitate immediately formed and it was collected by centrifugation. The precipitate was washed several times with deionized water, and then dried in an vacuum oven at 50 °C overnight.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. CuRA supported on MWCNTs (CuRA@MWCNT)
sections.text:
This procedure was similar to the synthesis of CuRA. Typically, 0.1 g
MWCNTs and 1mmol rubeanic acid were dispersed in 50mL of ethanol, followed by dropwise addition of 50mL of an aqueous solution with 1mmol Cu(NO3)2·3H2O under vigorous stirring. This process lasted for 24 h at room temperature. Subsequently, the gelatinous mixture was separated by centrifugation and it was followed by washing several times with deionized water. Finally, the product was dried at 50 °C under vacuum overnight. The product was named CuRA@MWCNT.
2.2.3. Preparation of Cu1.81S and Cu1.81S supported on MWCNTs (Cu1.81S@MWCNT)
Cu1.81S was prepared through the direct pyrolysis of CuRA. Typically, CuRA was put into a quartz boat, heated to 600 °C at a ramp rate of 3 °Cmin−1, and held for 2 h in a tube furnace under N2 flow (100mL min−1). The dark brown powder formed was identified as Cu1.81S.
Similarly, to obtain Cu1.81S@MWCNT, CuRA@MWCNT were placed in a quartz boat, heated to 600 °C at a ramp rate of 3 °Cmin−1, and held for 2 h under N2 flow (100mL min−1) in a tube furnace. After cooling to room temperature naturally, black powder was collected. The product was identified as Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600, where the last three digitals represent the pyrolysis temperature. In addition, Cu1.81S@MWCNT-400 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 were prepared by similar methods. The only difference among these catalysts was that Cu1.81S@MWCNT-400 was formed at 400 °C and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 was formed at 800 °C.
2.2.4. Preparation of oxide-modification Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 (Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD)
Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 were placed in a quartz boat in tube furnace and held at 200 °C for 3 h under flowing air (100 sccm). The product was identified as Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text: Nitrogen adsorption–desorption method was conducted using Autosorb iQ Station 1 to examine the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) specific surface area and pore parameters. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of samples were obtained using a SHIMADZU XRD-7000 powder polycrystalline X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (40 kV and 30mA) at a range of 10−80°, with a scanning speed of 5.0° min−1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo ESCALAB 250XI) was used to analyze the surface elemental compositions and electronic configurations of the products. All binding energies recorded for the samples were referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. Inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) was conducted on Varian 730-ES. Element Analysis (EA) was used to measure the C/S/O contents of samples on Elementar vario MICRO cube. Raman spectra were recorded with a LabRam HR800 UVRaman spectrometer integrated by JDbin-yvon Co., Ltd using a 514-nm laser. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were acquired with a Hitachi SU-8100 field emission scanning electron microscope. Powdered samples for SEM were dispersed in the dry form and deposited on carbon conductive tape before imaging. In addition, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), High-resolution TEM (HR-TEM), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping were performed with a FEI Talos F200S with an EDX spectroscope at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Before testing, all the sample powders were dispersed in ultra high purity ethanol. The suspension was dropped on a molybdenum grid and then the ethanol was evaporated. High-angle annular dark field (HAADF) mode was applied for STEM imaging and EDX mapping.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The electrochemical measurements were conducted in an sealed Htype cell (H-cell, 30mL for each compartment) separated by an cation exchange membrane (Nafion® 117, dupont, thickness 0.007 in.) using a
CHI 6043 electrochemical workstation (CH Instruments, Inc., USA). The three-electrode electrochemical setup comprised of a platinum gauze counter electrode, an Hg/HgO (1M KOH) reference electrode, and a glassy carbon electrode (GCE, 8mm in diameter) working electrode. In a typical procedure, 60 μL of homogeneous ink was prepared through adequate sonication of 5mg catalyst, 30 μL Nafion solution (5 wt%) and 970 μL ethanol, was pipetted onto a pre-polished GCE. Then the loaded GCE was dried in air at room temperature before use. To convert all of the potentials in the study to the RHE reference scale, the following formula was applied.
E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Hg/HgO) + 0.098 V+0.059 V × pH (1)

sections.heading: 2.5. CO2 reduction electrolysis and product analysis
sections.text:
During the CO2 reduction electrolysis, the electrolyte (0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution if not specified) in both compartments was stirred at 300 rpm. The current density results were normalized towards the geometric surface area of the GCE (0.5024 cm−2). Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were performed in N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 (pH=8.8) and CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 (pH=7.2) at a scan rate of 0.05 V s-1. The LSV curves exhibited in this paper were all compensated by resistance. Controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) measurements were performed at given potential for 60min after purging the electrolyte for 30min to saturate the solution with CO2. Before the controlled potential electrolysis, we activated the prepared electrode with fast cyclic voltammetry treatment, scan from 0.5 to -0.7 (vs RHE) at 0.1 V s-1, repeat 10 laps. During the measurements, CO2 gas was continuously delivered to the electrolytic cell at a flow rate of 15 ± 0.5mL min-1 and subsequently transported into the gas sampling loop (1mL) of a gas chromatograph (Superlab Smart GC) equipped with a packed column (Porapak N 80/100 mesh, 2m (L) × 1/8 in.(OD) ×2.1mm (OD) stainless steel), a thermal conductivity detector (for H2) and a flame ionization detector (for CO, CH4). The gas sample was analyzed every 15min to minimize the measurement error. All of the quantification of the gas products was completed with conversion factors derived from standard calibration gases. The liquid products were detected after electrolysis using a BRUKER AVANCE III 500MHz nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as an internal standard. After electrolysis, 500 μL of catholyte was removed from the H-cell with a syringe and then mixed with 100 μL D2O and 30 μL internal standard (include 1 vol% DMSO). Solvent presaturation techniques were performed to suppress the water peak and obtain the 1H spectrum, while formate was the only product. A typical NMR spectrum is shown in Fig. S1. To quantify the formate, a linear relationship between formate concentration and relative area of DMSO was implemented.

sections.heading: 3.1. Catalyst preparation
sections.text: To avoid the risk of using hydrogen sulfide, which is a lethal gas on humans, a facile two-step synthesis process was applied as shown in Scheme 1. The fabrication of multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) supported Cu1.81S hybrid catalysts (Cu1.81S@MWCNT-400/600/800) involved room-temperature synthesis and pyrolysis treatment at certain temperature, following which the oxide-modification Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-600 (Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD) were obtained through calcination of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 in air.

sections.heading: 3.2. Characterization
sections.text:
The nitrogen adsorption measurements (Fig. S19) indicates that the CuRA@MWCNT showed significant differences in surface area results when compared with pristine MWCNTs. The specific surface areas of MWCNTs and CuRA@MWCNT were measured to be 375.1 m2 g−1 and 174.2 m2 g−1, respectively, as reported in Table 1, revealing that the CuRA was successfully loaded onto the MWCNTs.
During the heating process, the precursors were decomposed to Cu1.81S particles, which are deposited onto the MWCNTs resulting in a Cu1.81S@MWCNT composite structure. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Cu1.81S@MWCNT formed at different temperature are shown in Fig. 1. The broad peak located at around 26.1° appeared in all the samples and it was assigned to the characteristic MWCNT (002) diffraction, while high diffraction peaks of Cu1.81S were detected at 2θ=27.6°, 29.5°, 31.6°, 32.5°, 37.5°, 39.0°, 45.4°, 46.1°, 48.5°, and 53.8°. The peaks correspond to the (203), (115), (016), (124), (130), (132), (135), (019), (227), and (144) planes of Cu1.81S (PDF#41−0959), respectively. It is noteworthy that two weak diffraction peaks at 35.5° and 36.5°, which correspond to the (11) plane of CuO and (111) of Cu2O, respectively, were detected for Cu1.81S@
Scheme 1. Schematic illustration of the preparation of Cu1.81S@MWCNT.
MWCNT-800 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD. It’s commonly understood that the copper oxides of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 are formed by the airoxidation of Cu particles generated by excessive decomposition during pyrolysis at temperatures as high as 800 °C [38]. In the synthesis of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD, mild oxidation conditions were applied to partly drive the Cu1.81S to copper oxides. The XRD results (Fig. 1) agree with the elemental analysis results (Table 2) that indicate the oxygen content of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD were much higher than the other composite materials. Subsequently, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis (Fig. S2) was used to assess the surface elemental compositions of prepared catalysts. The Cu 2p3/2 spectra for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600, Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 were fit with two peaks, indicating the presence of Cu(I) and Cu(II) as overlapping signals at 933 and 935 eV. These signals are ascribed to Cu1.81S and CuOx, respectively. As Fig. S2 shows, the level of Cu1.81S decreases and the CuOx increases following the order of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600, Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD, and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800, which is in accord with the results of the XRD analysis.
The investigation of the surface morphology and structure with prepared catalysts was conducted using both Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and Transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Representative SEM micrographs of handled MWCNT and CuRA@ MWCNT (Fig. S3) exhibit that the MWCNTs were totally enveloped by the precursor. Fig. S4 demonstrates that the CuRA loaded onto the surface of the MWCNTs was degraded slightly at 400 °C. When the thermal treatment temperature increases to 600 °C, significant levels of Cu1.81S particles are generated from the CuRA precursor and they are uniformly deposited on the MWCNTs as Fig. 2a demonstrates. Fig. 2b shows representative TEM micrographs of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600, exhibiting dispersed nanometer-sized particles on MWCNTs. The size of the Cu1.81S nanoparticles is approximately 57 nm as measured from the TEM micrographs (Fig. S5). A representative High-angle annular dark field-Scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM)
micrograph and the corresponding EDX maps of the Cu1.81S@MWCNT600 (Fig. 2c) indicate the uniform distribution of Cu and S in the nanoparticles and the widespread distribution of C, suggesting the formation of copper sulfides on MWCNTs (Cu1.81S@WMCNT-600). The composition of the particles seen in the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 samples was further evaluated using High-resolution Transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and representative results are shown in Figs. 2d and S6. The interplanar spacing of the particle lattice is in good agreement with the spacing of Cu1.81S planes. The inset in the TEM image in Fig. S6a shows the selected-area electron-diffraction (SAED) pattern, in which the bright circular rings correspond to (203), (124), (132), and (019) planes of Cu1.81S. This result confirms the good polycrystalline nature of the synthesized Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 sample, which is in accord with the XRD results. The geometric confinement of the Cu1.81S particles formed on MWCNTs is able to enhance their interfacial contact, thereby restraining the dissolution and agglomeration of the nanoparticles. This leads to improved electrocatalytic activity and stability. However, when the pyrolytic temperature reached 800 °C, the amount of coated nanoparticles (Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800) dramatically decreases as shown in Fig. S7, while the particle size significantly increases (average size =160 nm) as shown in Fig. S8. It is hypothesized that parts of the Cu1.81S particles decompose to Cu particles that are easily aggregated at the higher pyrolytic temperatures. [39,40] This
is followed by an unavoidable oxidation process upon exposure to air. Interestingly, the electron microscope analysis of the Cu1.81S@MWCNT600 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD samples indicates that there is no distinct variation in the morphology before and after the calcination in air (post calcination average size =55.5 nm) as shown in Figs. S9 and S10.
Raman analysis was performed to detect the level of defects in the MWCNTs as a function of the pyrolytic processing temperature. The Raman spectrum of pyrolyzed samples (Fig. S11) demonstrated a Dband (defective sp3 carbon) at 1352 cm−1 and a G-band (crystalline graphitic carbon) at 1574 cm-1 [41]. More specifically, the D band grew in intensity as the pyrolysis temperature was increased, along with a broadening of the G band with a shift to higher frequencies, indicating an increase in disorder. The ratio of the band intensities (ID/IG) reflect the defect level of the carbon base [42]. It is noted that the Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-800 has the highest ID/IG ratio (1.350) relative to 600 °C (1.282), 400 °C (1.221), and pristine MWCNTs (1.227). This confirms an increase in the defect level corresponding to an increase of the pyrolysis temperature. However, these defect sites are expected to act as adsorption sites for CO2 and active centers in CO2ER [43,44].

sections.heading: 3.3. Electrochemical reduction of CO2
sections.text:
To evaluate the CO2ER activity of Cu1.81S@MWNCT, Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements of the prepared catalysts/glassy
carbon electrodes (GCE) was conducted in N2 or CO2 saturated 0.5M KHCO3 electrolytes from -0.2 V to -1.2 V vs. RHE at a scan rate of 5mV s−1. As shown in Fig. S12, all of the polarization curves for the hybrid catalysts acquired in CO2-saturated electrolyte exhibit higher faradaic current densities than the corresponding curves in N2-saturated
electrolyte. The current density for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD show the most conspicuous improvement in CO2-saturated electrolyte compared with N2-saturated solution, indicating excellent CO2ER activity relative to the HER. It is reasoned that the faradaic currents obtained under the N2 atmosphere were attributed to the HER, while the faradaic currents in the CO2-saturated solution came from both the HER and CO2ER [45]. Additionally, the MWCNTs (Fig. 3a) show negligible current densities at all applied potentials and H2 is the only product. This suggests that it is the Cu1.81S nanoparticles rather than the MWCNTs that play a role in the CO2ER in all of the hybrid catalyst systems. Furthermore, the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD exhibit the highest current densities of all of the prepared catalysts, with minimal differences between the two. Coincidentally, the trends in the onset-potential results for the tested catalysts is similar to the trends for the LSV current density results. The onset-potential of Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-600-OD catalysts is as low as -0.47 V, which is more positive than the onset-potential for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-400 catalysts (-0.52 V), Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 catalysts (-0.56 V), and Cu1.81S (-0.59 V), and it is almost identical to the value for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 catalysts (-0.48 V). This highlights the synergistic effect of Cu1.81S and MWCNTs
to enhance the CO2ER. Subsequently, controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) was conducted
at various potentials for 1 h in a CO2-saturated, aqueous 0.5M KHCO3 solution using an airtight H-cell to analyze the product distribution resulting from the CO2ER. Under these reaction conditions, formate was detected as the only product from the CO2 reduction and H2 is the only byproduct due to the competitive HER. The faradaic efficiencies (FEs) were calculated based on the amounts of products produced and the quantities of charge passed during the experiment. Moreover, partial current density was used to evaluate the HER and CO2ER activities. Finally, CO2 dissolved in the catholyte was the reactant source for generating formate, not the bicarbonate, because only H2 was detected in the products that result from electrolysis in the N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte.
The faradaic efficiency towards formate (formate-FE) for the various Cu1.81S@MWCNT catalysts as a function of the applied potential are given in Fig. 3b. The formate-FE of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 reached 69 % at -0.67 V vs. RHE (jtotal = -3.84mA cm−1), and exhibited noteworthy performance in converting CO2 to formate over a wide range of potentials (> 47 %, from -0.57 to -0.87 V vs. RHE). Cu1.81S@MWCNT-400 showed relatively lower FEs over the range of potentials evaluated here (< 40 %, from -0.57 to -0.87 V vs. RHE). The distinct differences in these results is attributed to the amount of Cu1.81S particles that are loaded on the MWCNTs, due to the incomplete degradation of the precursor at 400 °C. If the synthesis conditions are optimized to the proper sintering temperature and time, the resulting product will have good electrochemical properties due to the generation of finer particles
with better crystallinity. Specifically, well-crystallized and uniformly sized Cu1.81S combined with the high specific surface area of MWCNTs promotes the CO2ER. It is worth noting that Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD catalysts, which are calcined in air at 200 °C after pyrolysis, are more competitive than Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 in enhancing the CO2ER. The formate-FE of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD reached nearly 82 % at -0.67 V vs. RHE (jtotal = -3.75mA cm−1) and showed remarkable activity for converting CO2 to formate across a wide range potentials (> 70 %, from -0.62 to -0.82 V vs. RHE). Additionally, when compared to Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600, the jHCOO- of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD increased, while the HER was suppressed as shown in Figs. 3c–d, S13. This reveals that the HER and the CO2ER compete on the same active sites of the catalysts and the oxidation process improved the electrocatalytic activity of CO2 while suppressing the HER.
Interestingly, the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 catalysts that contained significant levels of CuxO and moderate levels of Cu1.81S (confirmed by XRD) showed poorer performance (FEs< 42 %) when involved in the CO2ER. When compared to the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD results, the significant decrease in the fomate-FE for the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 catalysts can be ascribed to the large-sized Cu1.81S/CuxO hybrid particles formed by auto-agglomeration during the high-temperature pyrolysis process (as Figs. S7 and S9 show). The dramatical drop in surface area and pore volume (Table 1), along with the decreased active species, hinder the mass transport, thereby hampering the formation of formate.
The double-layer capacitance (Cdl) experiment evaluates the relative number of active sites of catalysts and the value of Cdl was estimated
through varied CV scan rates (Fig. S14). The Cdl for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD is approximately 16.6 m F cm−2, which is 1.6 and 21.3 times greater than the values obtained for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800 (10.3 m F cm−2) and Cu1.81S (0.78 m F cm−2) (Fig. 4a). The Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 catalyst reaches a similar Cdl, 16.4 m F cm−2, to that obtained for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD. This result is consistent with the specific surface areas determined by nitrogen BET measurements (Table 1). The Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 (243.5 m2 g-1) and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD (249.0 m2 g-1) show the highest and similar specific surface areas of all of the prepared catalysts. Similar Cdl and specific surface areas measured for Cu1.81S@MWCNT600 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD catalysts reveal that the mild lowtemperature oxidation process maintains the primal morphology and structure of the samples, which is in agreement with the results of the electron microscope evaluation. The high Cdl for Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD confirms the existence of a large amount of active sites, which will enhance the adsorption of CO2 and facilitate the CO2ER. In addition, the distinct difference in the Cdl between Cu1.81S particles and Cu1.81S@MWCNT reveals that the MWCNTs not only provide channels for transporting reactants and products, but also enables electron interactions with the active phase of the catalyst. The results match well with the results from the LSVs that found the onsetpotential is Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD ≈ Cu1.81S@MWCNT600<Cu1.81S@MWCNT-800<Cu1.81S. Interestingly, the current density of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD at -0.87 V vs. RHE is only 2 times that of the Cu1.81S, while the Cdl of the former is around 20 times that of the later. This is due to the inevitable mass transport limitation on the
Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD that allows only a fraction of the active sites to participate in the CO2 reduction.
Furthermore, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed to evaluate the charge transfer resistance of the various samples. Fig. 4b demonstrates that the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD has the lowest charge transfer impedance (Rct) with the order being Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD<Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600<Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-800< <Cu1.81S. This result is consistent with the experimental observation that Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD has the highest capacitance and highest current density. Prior research [46,47] indicated that catalysts with lower Rct have lower charge-transfer resistance between the reactant and the surface of catalyst, providing a fast pathway for transferring electrons to CO2 in order to generating CO2·− intermediates.
The Cu-S based hybrid catalysts solely convert CO2 to formate, which is in stark contrast to pristine Cu that is able to produce various products including CO, formate, hydrocarbons (methane, ethylene, ethane, etc), and alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propanol, etc) through the CO2ER [20–22]. Nørskov and co-workers [48] proposed a plausible mechanistic pathways for CO2 conversion over a pristine Cu surface on the basis of density functional theory (DFT) calculations. First, CO2 is reduced into either *COOH or *OCHO intermediate species via one electron and proton transfer. For the formation of CO, CO2 is protonated to *COOH rather than *OCHO. Subsequently, the *COOH is further reduced to *CO, which can desorb to form CO, or successively converted to hydrocarbons or alcohols (*COOH can be also converted to HCOO−). On the other hand, *OCHO can only be converted to
HCOO− due to its geometric characteristics. In order to study the effect of active components on the CO2ER mechanism, especially the formation pathway for formate, the Tafel slopes for the jHCOO− on Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-600 and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD were investigated under low overpotentials as shown in Fig. 4c. The Tafel slopes for Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-600 (126 mV dec-1) and Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD (120 mV dec-1) are similar, which agrees with the results of the polarization tests. These values are on the order of magnitude of 118 mV dec-1, suggesting that the single electron transfer process to form *CO− is the rate-determining step [49].
Finally, the stability of the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD catalyst was tested over an extended time. At a constant potential of -0.67 V vs. RHE in a CO2-saturated aqueous bicarbonate solution (Fig. 4d), the current density maintained a steady value of -3.75 mA cm−2 for the initial two hours, then slowly increased to -4.2 mA cm−2. Additionally, the FE of formate fluctuated around 80–84 % throughout the duration of the long-term electrolysis experiment. The impact of the extended period of performance on the catalyst structure was further investigated. To evaluate the change in resistance, EIS test was conducted as shown in Fig. S15, suggesting that the charge transfer impedance of Cu1.81S@ MWCNT-600-OD decreased after long-term electrolysis. XRD analysis (Fig. S16) indicates that the used Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD exhibits minimal differences compared to the fresh catalyst except for some signal intensity drop. Additionally, XPS analysis (Fig. S17) exhibits that small amounts of Cu have been reduced during the long-term electrolysis. To investigate variations in morphology and structure further, SEM analysis of Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD over different electrolysis times was performed (Fig. 5). This reveals that the MWCNT-support structure is retained, while the Cu1.81S particles gradually aggregate (Fig. 5a) and reform (Fig. 5d) into a needle-like dendritic structures.
Weng et al. [50] found that copper-based materials reconstruct themselves during the electroreduction of CO2. It is reasonable to
assume that the observed morphological changes here are a result of the restructuring processes taking place during the long-term electrolysis. The dendritic nanostructures result in the formation of a metal-based electrode with hierarchical porosity and large specific surface area, thus providing more active surface sites that significantly improve the electrocatalytic performance. It is hypothesized that proper levels of copper oxide play the vital role in the morphology restructure, since dendritic structures are not detected in used Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 catalysts during SEM analysis (Fig. S18). Therefore, rational molecular structure design of catalysts (e.g., formation of smaller size nanoclusters or needle-like clusters) will be able to expose more active sites and enhance the current density and electrocatalytic performance. Furthermore, copper oxide modification, formed with a mild oxidation process, is a facile pathway for assisting copper sulfide in-situ restructuring to needle-like dendritic structure with enhanced performance.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In general, Cu1.81S nanoparticles deposited on MWCNTs were synthesized through pyrolysis of a hydrothermally prepared precursor, uniformly coated on the MWCNT support without surface functionalization. The Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600 catalyst exhibited excellent performance in the CO2 reduction to formate rather than the HER. The strong selectivity and low onset-potential are attributed to the combination of the uniform dispersion of Cu1.81S particles, large specific surface area, and fast mass and electron transfer through the MWNCT support. With a mild oxidation process, the Cu1.81S@MWCNT-600-OD showed further enhanced catalytic activity, with a high formate-FE of 82 %. Further stability testing and morphology investigation indicated that the presence of copper oxide species promotes restructuring and the resulting needle-like dendritic structure concentrates the current density, and is
therefore likely responsible for the improvement in the formation of formate. These results provide a facile pathway to synthesize cost-effective and abundant CO2ER catalysts and morphology reconstruction through low-temperature oxidation is one useful method to enhance the CO2ER performance of nanocatalysts.
